newsitem.title: USA: Study finds nearly 1,200 U.S.-Mexico border deaths.
newsitem.headline: Study finds nearly 1,200 U.S.-Mexico border deaths.

text.p: Nearly 1,200 people died while crossing illegally into the United States from Mexico between 1993 and 1996, many by drowning, according to a study released on Monday.
The number may increase as the United States beefs up its enforcement of illegal immigration, the study by the Centre for Immigration Research at the University of Houston said.

It said of the estimated 1,185 deaths, 851 were caused by drowning, particularly along the Rio Grande, which separates Texas from Mexico. The second leading cause of death was auto-pedestrian accidents, which killed 90 people.

"Environmental" deaths -- from dehydration and exposure -- were on the rise because would-be immigrants were crossing the 2,000-mile-long (3,200 km) border at more remote locations to escape detection by U.S. border patrols, the study said.
"The number of (environmental) deaths in San Diego County (California) rose from none in 1993 to 16 in 1996," the study said. "Environmental" causes were blamed for 58 deaths.

The San Diego area was the most lethal of the 19 border sectors included in the study. Researchers said 193 people died there during the study period, which coincided with stepped-up efforts to put a clamp on illegal immigration.

Similar escalated enforcement campaigns were now underway in Texas, with the result that it will become "more difficult and more dangerous for would-be crossers," University of Houston sociology professor Jacqueline Hagan said.
"Our study suggests that there needs to be more money funnelled toward lifesaving operations," she said.
Also, the researchers suggested that U.S. immigration authorities should increase enforcement operations in dangerous areas to discourage crossings in those places and reduce deaths.
The data was gathered by poring over records in 19 sectors along the border, but researchers said many immigrant deaths go unnoticed or unrecorded by officials.

The study was the first to look at illegal immigrant deaths along the entire U.S-Mexico border. A study released last year by the research centre looked only at deaths along the Texas-Mexico border, where 3,200 illegal immigrants died between 1985 and 1994, most from drowning.
